title: SendAs grants by a tenant identity administrator
lede: An AI-assist workflow escalated four days of activity on this account, citing privileged admin actions, a SendAs delegation, and missing sign-in telemetry. All three grounds were tested against the tenant's own data. None of them survive.

verdict.text: Routine identity administration by the person whose job it is. No containment action required; the rule that produced these incidents needs tuning.

grounds.intro: Each claim below is quoted from the AI-assist workflow, followed by what the tenant's data actually shows.

items.claim: No sign-in telemetry to validate origin.
items.finding: This is a **tenant-wide collection gap**, not a property of this account. `AzureSigninLogs` returns **0 rows** over 30 days, while `Office365` holds **2,922,289** and `AzureAuditLogs` **17,543**. The absence applies identically to every user on the tenant, including every benign one, so it carries no discriminating power at all.

The tenant recorded **14** `Add-RecipientPermission` events in 30 days. **12 were hers**, spread across **8 separate days** from 08-25 to 09-22, every one of them `AccessRights: SendAs` on internal tenant objects. One grant every two to three days, sustained for a month, is a standing pattern — the shape of a staffing firm delegating branch mailboxes — not an event.

items.claim: 250–324 directory actions by a Global Administrator.
items.finding: That is her baseline. Identity-admin volume runs **5 to 93 operations every working day** for the full month: 150 `Update user.`, 117 `AddedToGroup`, 86 group removals, 76 password resets, 68 `Set-Mailbox`. The flagged days are **not spikes** — see below.

score_table.title: The score does not follow the activity
score_table.intro: If the incidents tracked what she did, the two columns would rise together. They do not. 09-21 scored 5800 on *fewer* operations than 09-09 scored 600 on.

callout.title: What is actually driving the score
callout.body: Every one of these summaries carries `ML_NEW_USER` — the first-seen term. The rule fires on the novelty of the *target* user, not on the risk of the action. An administrator whose job is touching users she has not touched before will trip it indefinitely.

base_rate.title: She is not an outlier among her peers
base_rate.intro: The same rules fire for a small cohort of administrators on this tenant. The highest score in the window belongs to someone else.
base_rate.caption: Base rate across the 30-day window, by rule.

items.title: No inbox rules.
items.body: Zero by this account, against 31 `Set-InboxRule` and 14 `New-InboxRule` elsewhere on the tenant.

items.title: No mail forwarding or transport rules.
No OAuth consents or service principals.
items.body: Zero, against 11 consents and 7 service principals elsewhere.

items.title: No unusual access.
items.body: 192 sign-ins from a single stable IPv4 spanning the entire month, plus one IPv6 /64 with rotating privacy suffixes. No new geography, no new ISP.

callouts.title: On the “ISP discrepancy”
callouts.body: The Microsoft-owned addresses the workflow flagged appear on *cmdlet* records, not on her sign-ins. Exchange Online writes its own service infrastructure as the client address when an administrative cmdlet runs. Her interactive sessions carry her own connection throughout, and every event is `ExternalAccess: false`.

recommendation: Close benign, with no containment. The finding worth acting on is the detection, not the account: these rules raise an incident every time an administrator touches a user for the first time, which for this cohort is continuous. Tune the `ML_NEW_USER` contribution on admin-operation rules rather than the operations themselves.
Separately, `AzureSigninLogs` is empty tenant-wide. That is a real gap and worth fixing on its own merits — but it is an ingestion issue, not evidence about any user.

footer.evidence: Office365 (2.92M rows), AzureAuditLogs (17.5K), behavior summaries (127 hits)
